title: What is a data lake — a storage place (like S3/HDFS) where you dump ALL raw data (structured + unstructured) cheaply, and process it later — vs a data warehouse (like Snowflake/Redshift) which stores clean, organized data ready for queries?
shortTitle: What is a data lake (vs a data warehouse)

s1_definition.profdef: A data lake is a low-cost storage system, typically object storage like S3 or HDFS, that holds vast amounts of raw data in its original form — structured, semi-structured, and unstructured — using schema-on-read, so structure is applied only when the data is queried. A data warehouse is a structured analytical database like Snowflake or Redshift that stores cleaned, modelled, schema-on-write data optimized for fast SQL analytics. The lake is cheap raw storage; the warehouse is expensive query-ready storage.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has two rooms. The data lake is a giant cheap warehouse where every raw document is dumped as it comes in — card logs, scanned cheque images, call recordings, app clickstreams — all thrown in boxes with no sorting, because storage is cheap and you might need it later. The data warehouse is the neat records room upstairs where only clean, labelled, filed statements live, arranged so a manager can instantly pull "Rajesh's spend by month". The lake keeps everything just in case; the warehouse keeps the polished subset ready to answer questions fast.
s1_definition.oneliner: A data lake cheaply stores all raw data for later; a data warehouse stores clean, modelled data ready to query fast.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A data lake is a low-cost storage system, typically object storage like S3 or HDFS, that holds vast amounts of raw data in its original form — structured, semi-structured, and unstructured — using schema-on-read, so structure is applied only when the data is queried. A data warehouse is a structured analytical database like Snowflake or Redshift that stores cleaned, modelled, schema-on-write data optimized for fast SQL analytics. The lake is cheap raw storage; the warehouse is expensive query-ready storage.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has two rooms. The data lake is a giant cheap warehouse where every raw document is dumped as it comes in — card logs, scanned cheque images, call recordings, app clickstreams — all thrown in boxes with no sorting, because storage is cheap and you might need it later. The data warehouse is the neat records room upstairs where only clean, labelled, filed statements live, arranged so a manager can instantly pull "Rajesh's spend by month". The lake keeps everything just in case; the warehouse keeps the polished subset ready to answer questions fast.

**One line to remember:** A data lake cheaply stores all raw data for later; a data warehouse stores clean, modelled data ready to query fast.

sections.s2_technical:
A data lake is built on cheap, massively scalable object storage. Its defining trait is schema-on-read: you store bytes now and decide their structure only when you read them. That makes it ideal for landing everything — raw JSON events, CSV files, Parquet, images, logs — without an upfront modelling step. Lakes handle structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data equally. The flexibility is the strength and the danger: without governance a lake becomes a "data swamp" where nobody knows what is in which folder or whether it is trustworthy. A typical lake read in Spark is `spark.read.parquet("s3://bank-lake/raw/txns/dt=2024-10-29/")`, pointing at a partitioned path.

A data warehouse is a managed analytical database using schema-on-write: you define tables and types up front, and data must conform before it is loaded. It is column-oriented and heavily optimized for analytical scans and aggregations, so queries like "total card spend per region last quarter" run fast over billions of rows. Modelling matters here — star schemas with fact and dimension tables are common. The warehouse holds clean, conformed, business-ready data, which is why analysts and BI tools point at it. A warehouse query is plain SQL such as `SELECT account_id, SUM(amount) FROM fact_transactions WHERE txn_month = '2024-10' GROUP BY account_id`.

The practical relationship is that they work together. Raw data lands in the lake cheaply, then ETL or ELT cleans and models a refined subset into the warehouse for serving. Many banks organize the lake into zones — raw, cleansed, and curated — to add governance. A senior nuance is the rise of the lakehouse, which puts warehouse-like features (ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel) on top of lake storage using table formats like Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, or Hudi, giving you one platform instead of copying data between two. Cost and access patterns drive the choice: the lake is pennies per gigabyte but slower and less governed, the warehouse costs more but delivers governed, interactive SQL, and the lakehouse tries to blend both.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants to keep every raw event forever and cheaply, including messy records it has not modelled yet, because a future fraud model might need them. This is exactly a data lake — dump raw records now, apply structure later.

Problem 2 — Analysts need fast, clean answers like "total spend per account" without wading through raw mess. This is exactly a data warehouse — store a curated, conformed subset ready to query.

Problem 3 — The bank needs a job that promotes data from the lake to the warehouse by cleaning and modelling it. This is exactly the lake-to-warehouse ETL.

The mini-project models `LakeRecord` as raw data (may be invalid) and `WarehouseRow` as curated data. `DataLake` stores everything with `dump()`. `DataWarehouse` stores only conformed rows with `insert()` and answers `totalByAccount()`. `Curation` promotes lake records to the warehouse, dropping invalid ones. The demo dumps raw records into the lake, curates them into the warehouse, and shows the warehouse answering a fast aggregate query while the lake still holds everything including the rejects.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is four raw records dumped into the lake: R1 (Rajesh, 1200), R2 (Rajesh, 800), R3 (Priya, 5000), and R4 (Priya, null amount — junk).

Step 1 — Dump into lake. All four records, including the null-amount junk R4, are stored in the lake with no validation. The lake now holds four records because its job is to keep everything cheaply.

Step 2 — Curation reads the lake. The promotion job iterates every lake record. It applies schema-on-read logic now, validating each one as it is pulled.

Step 3 — Curation filters. R4 has a null amount, so it is skipped with a warning. The junk stays in the lake but never enters the warehouse.

Step 4 — Curation loads the warehouse. R1, R2, R3 are conformed into `WarehouseRow` objects and inserted. The warehouse now holds three clean rows.

Step 5 — Fast query. The warehouse answers an OLAP aggregate instantly: Rajesh 1200 + 800 = 2000, Priya 5000. Meanwhile the lake still holds all four records, so if a future model needs even the junk, it is preserved.

```
INFO: Lake holds 4 raw records (including junk)
INFO: CURATION: promoting valid lake records into the warehouse
WARNING: Skipping invalid lake record R4
INFO: Warehouse holds 3 curated rows
INFO: === FAST OLAP QUERY: total by account ===
INFO: SAV2001 = 2000.00
INFO: CUR3001 = 5000.00
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A data lake is a low-cost, massively scalable storage system, usually object storage like S3 or HDFS, that holds all your raw data in its original form, whether structured, semi-structured, or unstructured. Its defining trait is schema-on-read, meaning you store the bytes now and apply structure only when you query them, which is why a lake is perfect for landing everything cheaply in case you need it later. A data warehouse, by contrast, is a structured analytical database like Snowflake or Redshift that uses schema-on-write, so data must be cleaned and modelled before it is loaded. It is column-oriented and tuned for fast analytical scans, so business queries run quickly.

They are not competitors; they work together. Raw data lands in the lake cheaply, then ETL or ELT cleans and models a refined subset into the warehouse for serving, and many banks organize the lake into raw, cleansed, and curated zones to add governance and avoid turning it into a data swamp where nobody trusts anything. A senior point I always raise is the lakehouse, which uses table formats like Delta Lake, Iceberg, or Hudi to put warehouse-like ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and time travel directly on top of lake storage, so you get one platform instead of constantly copying data between two.

In my project at the National Bank of India we used both. The lake kept every raw event forever and cheaply, including messy or incomplete records, because a future fraud model might one day need them. A curation job then promoted only the valid records into the warehouse, dropping junk like a null-amount row, and the warehouse answered fast aggregate queries such as total spend per account for Rajesh and Priya. The important design idea was that the junk stayed safely in the lake but was never allowed to pollute the governed warehouse, which gives the bank both cheap completeness and trustworthy, interactive analytics.
